beats.say: Nine in ten: undergraduates at one college experience phantom phone vibrations.
The sensation appeared as phantom pager syndrome in a 1996 Dilbert comic strip before mobiles were everywhere.
The earliest published use of phantom vibration syndrome appeared in 2003, and the Macquarie Dictionary crowned it word of the year in 2012.
Carrying a mobile for just one month to a year is enough for these false buzzes to start happening to you.
Humans are naturally sensitive to tones between 1,000 and 6,000 hertz, which is the range where many phone alerts sit.

facts: In 1996, cartoonist Scott Adams referenced the sensation in the comic strip Dilbert as phantom pager syndrome.
The earliest published use of the term phantom vibration syndrome dates to 2003.
In 2012, phantom vibration syndrome was chosen as the Australian Macquarie Dictionary word of the year.
Researcher Michelle Drouin found that almost 9 out of 10 undergraduates at her college experienced phantom vibrations.
Vibrations typically begin occurring after carrying a phone for between one month and one year.
Humans are particularly sensitive to auditory tones between 1000 and 6000 hertz.
